title: Differential effects of GPT-based tools on comprehension of standardized passages
extended_summary:
This study examined whether GPT-based educational tools improve or hinder reading comprehension, and whether effects differ by students’ baseline ability. The authors note that AI tools are already widely used in education, but empirical evidence on their learning effects is limited. They focused on standardized reading comprehension as a foundational academic skill and tested whether AI support benefits lower-performing learners while potentially undermining higher-performing learners.

The intervention consisted of four GPT-4-based tools: an AI-generated summary, an AI-generated outline, a Q&A tutor chatbot, and a Socratic discussion chatbot. In a pre-registered randomized within-subject cross-over online experiment, participants completed five ACT-style reading comprehension conditions in a single session: four AI-tool conditions and one no-AI control. Passage order and condition order were randomized, and comprehension was measured using standardized 10-item ACT-derived quizzes.

The population was 195 college-aged adults (ages 18–22) in the United States recruited through Prolific after exclusions from an initial 228 participants. The study took place online through a custom web portal and used standardized ACT reading passages. Participants were split into lower- and higher-performing groups primarily based on control-passage performance, with SAT/ACT scores used as a secondary validation split.

The main conclusion was that GPT-based tools had strongly differential effects by baseline performance. Across the control-based split, all four AI tools improved comprehension for lower-performing participants but reduced comprehension for higher-performing participants. The Socratic chatbot showed the largest gains for lower performers, while the summary tool produced the largest declines for higher performers. The authors conclude that AI tools may help struggling learners but that universal implementation could unintentionally harm stronger readers, so deployment should be targeted and tested cautiously.

identified_tools.name: AI-generated summaries
identified_tools.description: A GPT-based summarization tool that generates condensed versions of reading passages.
identified_tools.use_case: Participants viewed a GPT-generated summary of an ACT-derived reading passage in place of the full passage before completing a 10-item reading comprehension quiz, compared with a no-AI control and other GPT-based supports.

findings.finding_summary: Using a subgroup split based on control-passage performance, the summary tool improved quiz accuracy for lower-performing participants: 55.4% (SD 18.7) with summary versus 44.9% (SD 15.8) in control, t(70)=3.8, p<0.001, d=0.45. The paper notes this positive pattern for lower performers was not robust across alternative subgroup definitions.

Using the control-passage subgroup split, the summary tool worsened reading comprehension for higher-performing participants: 66.5% (SD 18.4) with summary versus 82.5% (SD 10.5) in control, t(123)=9.2, p<0.001, d=0.83.
Using the SAT/ACT-based subgroup split, the summary tool did not significantly affect quiz performance for lower SAT/ACT performers: 61.5% (SD 18.3) with summary versus 66.2% (SD 22.9) in control.
Among participants who had not taken the SAT/ACT, the summary tool did not significantly affect quiz performance: 56.8% (SD 16.6) with summary versus 62.1% (SD 20.8) in control.

Using the SAT/ACT-based subgroup split, the summary tool worsened quiz performance for higher SAT/ACT performers: 67.6% (SD 20.9) with summary versus 76.5% (SD 20.2) in control, t(70)=2.9, p=0.005, d=0.35.

identified_tools.name: AI-generated outlines
identified_tools.description: A GPT-based outlining tool that reorganizes reading passages into structured outlines.
identified_tools.use_case: Participants read an ACT-derived passage presented in GPT-generated outline form before completing a 10-item reading comprehension quiz, compared with a no-AI control and other GPT-based supports.

findings.finding_summary: Using a subgroup split based on control-passage performance, the outline tool improved quiz accuracy for lower-performing participants: 60.0% (SD 21.0) with outline versus 44.9% (SD 15.8) in control, t(70)=6.3, p<0.001, d=0.74.

Using the control-passage subgroup split, the outline tool decreased quiz accuracy for higher-performing participants: 72.4% (SD 19.2) with outline versus 82.5% (SD 10.5) in control, t(123)=5.7, p<0.001, d=0.51.
Using the SAT/ACT-based subgroup split, the outline tool did not significantly affect quiz performance for lower SAT/ACT performers: 67.3% (SD 17.6) with outline versus 66.2% (SD 22.9) in control.
Among participants who had not taken the SAT/ACT, the outline tool did not significantly affect quiz performance: 61.9% (SD 25.3) with outline versus 62.1% (SD 20.8) in control.
For higher SAT/ACT performers, the outline tool showed a non-significant difference in quiz performance: 73.0% (SD 18.6) with outline versus 76.5% (SD 20.2) in control.

identified_tools.name: Q&A tutor chatbot
identified_tools.description: A GPT-based tutoring chatbot that answers learners' questions about a reading passage.
identified_tools.use_case: Participants read a full ACT-derived passage with access to a GPT-based question-answering tutor chatbot before completing a 10-item reading comprehension quiz, compared with a no-AI control and other GPT-based supports.

findings.finding_summary: Using a subgroup split based on control-passage performance, the Q&A tutor improved quiz accuracy for lower-performing participants: 56.2% (SD 19.0) with the tutor versus 44.9% (SD 15.8) in control, t(70)=4.2, p<0.001, d=0.50.

Using the control-passage subgroup split, the Q&A tutor reduced quiz accuracy for higher-performing participants: 75.1% (SD 19.0) with the tutor versus 82.5% (SD 10.5) in control, t(123)=4.1, p<0.001, d=0.37.
Using the SAT/ACT-based subgroup split, the Q&A tutor did not significantly affect quiz performance for lower SAT/ACT performers: 66.9% (SD 21.9) with the tutor versus 66.2% (SD 22.9) in control.
Among participants who had not taken the SAT/ACT, the Q&A tutor did not significantly affect quiz performance: 61.7% (SD 21.4) with the tutor versus 62.1% (SD 20.8) in control.
For higher SAT/ACT performers, the Q&A tutor did not significantly affect quiz performance: 74.4% (SD 18.3) with the tutor versus 76.5% (SD 20.2) in control.

identified_tools.name: Socratic discussion chatbot
identified_tools.description: A GPT-based tutoring chatbot that engages learners in Socratic dialogue about a reading passage.
identified_tools.use_case: Participants read a full ACT-derived passage while interacting with a GPT-based Socratic discussion chatbot before completing a 10-item reading comprehension quiz, compared with a no-AI control and other GPT-based supports.

findings.finding_summary: Using a subgroup split based on control-passage performance, the Socratic chatbot produced the largest improvement for lower-performing participants: 63.0% (SD 18.7) with the chatbot versus 44.9% (SD 15.8) in control, t(70)=7.2, p<0.001, d=0.86.

Using the control-passage subgroup split, the Socratic chatbot decreased quiz accuracy for higher-performing participants: 76.3% (SD 17.9) with the chatbot versus 82.5% (SD 10.5) in control, t(123)=3.7, p<0.001, d=0.33.

Using the SAT/ACT-based subgroup split, the Socratic chatbot improved quiz accuracy for lower SAT/ACT performers: 71.7% (SD 20.4) with the chatbot versus 66.2% (SD 22.9) in control, t(70)=2.2, p=0.03, d=0.26.
Among participants who had not taken the SAT/ACT, the Socratic chatbot improved reading comprehension: 70.2% (SD 18.4) with the chatbot versus 62.1% (SD 20.8) in control, t(52)=2.5, p=0.017, d=0.34.
For higher SAT/ACT performers, the Socratic chatbot showed a non-significant difference in quiz performance: 72.1% (SD 18.8) with the chatbot versus 76.5% (SD 20.2) in control.

quality_tier_rationale: This was a pre-registered randomized within-subject cross-over experiment with a no-AI control and standardized outcome measures, which strengthens causal inference. However, concerns remain due to the short single-session duration, online convenience sample from Prolific, and attrition/exclusions reducing the final sample.
impact_tier_rationale: Effects were substantial but mixed: AI tools improved outcomes for lower-performing participants while worsening outcomes for higher-performing participants. Because the intervention showed both positive and negative impacts rather than a clear overall benefit, the overall impact tier is best classified as unclear/mixed.
